summary: Specifies an extended version of the Telnet Remote Flow Control Option from RFC 1080, adding the RESTART-ANY and RESTART-XON suboptions.

eli5.summary: Telnet lets you use a distant computer. This option lets the two sides say stop and go for the text, and this version adds more ways to restart it.

questions: what is the telnet remote flow control option
subtitle: How a Telnet host tells the user's Telnet client when to turn terminal flow control off and on, and when output may restart.

tldr.problem: Software flow control steals the XOFF and XON characters, but host programs such as editors sometimes need to receive every character. The Telnet client does the flow control, so the host has no way to switch it off.
tldr.mechanism: The option TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL (code 33) lets the host send subnegotiations that turn flow control off or on, and choose whether any character or only XON restarts output.
tldr.outcome: This version obsoletes RFC 1080 by adding the RESTART-ANY and RESTART-XON suboptions. The RFC does not discuss security.

facts.label: Default
facts.value: WONT and DONT (no flow control information exchanged)

today: RFC 1372 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1080. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Flow Control Needs a Switch
sections.content:
RFC 1372 is about flow control of data going from the Telnet process to the attached terminal. There are two common kinds. Hardware flow control uses dedicated wires. Software flow control sends special characters on the same path as normal data, most commonly XOFF (control-S) to stop output and XON (control-Q) to start it again.

The option matters mainly for software flow control, because it takes over one or two characters. Host software often needs the user to be able to type every ASCII character, and some editors use XOFF and XON as ordinary commands. Operating systems therefore let programs disable flow control, so those characters arrive as normal input.

In a Telnet session the user Telnet process, not the host, does the flow control. So the host needs a way to pass its flow control status to that process. Many systems also let the user choose whether only XON, or any typed character, restarts output; this RFC carries that choice too.
sections.eli5: Two special keys act like a pause button and a play button. Some games need those keys for something else, so the computer far away needs a way to tell your terminal to ignore the buttons for a while.

sections.title: Command Names and Meanings
sections.content:
The option is called TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and has option code 33. It has four subnegotiation commands: OFF (0), ON (1), RESTART-ANY (2) and RESTART-XON (3). None of them carries any extra data.

The usual Telnet negotiation verbs mean the following here:

  • WILL: the sender is willing to enable and disable flow control on command.
  • WONT: the sender refuses to be toggled this way. This implies nothing about whether it uses flow control.
  • DO: the sender is willing to send commands that enable and disable flow control.
  • DONT: the sender refuses to send such commands.

A subnegotiation takes the form IAC SB TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL command IAC SE. OFF and ON ask the receiver to disable or enable flow control. RESTART-ANY asks that, while flow control is enabled, any character except another XOFF restarts output. RESTART-XON asks that only the XON character restarts it.
sections.eli5: There are four little messages: 'flow control off', 'flow control on', 'any key restarts', and 'only the go key restarts'. Each one is a tiny note with no extra writing on it.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use the Option
sections.content:
Using the option takes two phases. In the first, the two Telnet processes agree with a WILL and DO exchange that one of them will toggle flow control. Normally there is only one such exchange per session. Subnegotiations must not be sent until DO and WILL have been exchanged.

Either side may turn the option off by sending WONT or DONT. After that no more subnegotiations may be sent unless another DO and WILL exchange re-enables the option. If the option is disabled this way, flow control may revert to an implementation-defined default, so a program must not assume it stays in the state of the last subnegotiation.

The default is WONT TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL DONT TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL, meaning no flow control information is exchanged in either direction.
sections.eli5: First, both sides agree they will use the pause and play notes. Until they agree, nobody sends them. If one side changes its mind, the notes stop until they agree again.

sections.title: Who Controls What
sections.content:
Once the hosts have exchanged WILL and DO, the sender of the DO is free to send the subnegotiations. Normally that is a host, and the other end is a user Telnet process connected to a terminal, so the protocol is normally asymmetric. It may be used in both directions without confusion.

As soon as the exchange completes, the sender of the WILL must enable flow control, so that flow control begins in a known state. Whether output restarts only on XON or on any character starts in a system-dependent state, to stay consistent with older implementations that do not know the restart suboptions. The sender of the DO should send either RESTART-ANY or RESTART-XON to put the restart behaviour into a known state.

Some clients cannot support both restart modes and then ignore these commands. The server is not told, but a client should try to honor the requested state. Subnegotiations with command codes other than the four defined should be silently ignored, because more commands may be added later.

Normally the XOFF and XON characters are not passed on to the server. They are eaten by the terminal driver between the client and the terminal. With RESTART-ANY, the typed character that restarts output is usually not eaten, unless it is the XON character.
sections.eli5: The computer far away is usually the boss and your terminal follows. When they first agree, your side turns the pause button on so everyone starts from the same place.

sections.title: An Example Session
sections.content:
The RFC gives one exchange. The server sends IAC DO TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and the client answers IAC WILL TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL. The server may now send commands. The client must by now have enabled flow control, but whether restart is on XON only or on any character is client specific.

The server then sends RESTART-ANY, and the client should allow output to restart on any typed character if it can. Finally the server sends OFF followed by ON.

The option does not tell the DO side which characters the WILL side should use for XON and XOFF. The LINEMODE option, defined in RFC 1184, already supplies that.
sections.eli5: The server asks, 'Can I control your pause button?' The client says yes. Then the server says 'any key can restart', and later turns the pause button off and on again.

messages.label: IAC DO TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL
messages.note: Server offers to send flow control commands.

messages.label: IAC WILL TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL
messages.note: Client agrees and must now have flow control enabled.

messages.label: SB ... RESTART-ANY IAC SE
messages.note: Any character should now restart output, if supported.

items.label: RESTART-ANY
items.desc: Any character except another XOFF restarts output.

items.label: RESTART-XON
items.desc: Only the XON character restarts output.
